flawed_step: The natural proof uses Tutte's condition, as in Petersen's proof. Take S ⊆ V and an odd component C of G−S. Since the graph is cubic, 3|C| − 2|E(C)| is odd, so the number of edges from C to S is odd. The next step claims this number is at least 3, which would give 3·odd(G−S) ≤ 3|S|. That step needs the graph to be bridgeless (2-edge-connected). If the graph has a bridge, C can be joined to S by a single edge, so the inequality odd(G−S) ≤ |S| does not follow. Here the proof cannot be justified.
counterexample: Sylvester graph (16 vertices). Start with a central vertex v. Build three copies of a gadget: take K4 on {a,b,c,d}, subdivide the edge ab with a new vertex x, and join x to v. In each gadget, a, b, c and d have degree 3 and x has degree 3 (a, b, v). v also has degree 3. The graph is simple, connected and cubic. Removing S={v} leaves three components with 5 vertices each, which are odd. Since 3 > |S| = 1, Tutte's condition fails, so there is no perfect matching.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. The parity argument shows that each odd component of G−S sends an odd number of edges to S. The bound of at least 3 such edges needs bridgelessness. The Sylvester-type cubic graph above is connected but has bridges, and it breaks Tutte's condition with S={v}: three odd components against |S|=1. So it has no perfect matching, and the bridgeless hypothesis cannot be dropped.
